topic.subject: social
topic.title: The Earth in the solar system
topic.scope: planets, Earth as a unique planet, Moon, asteroids, meteoroids, satellites

nodes.name: Asteroids are between Mars and Jupiter

misconceptions.statement: Planets move in perfect circles around the Sun.
misconceptions.why: Students often simplify complex geometry to familiar shapes like circles.
misconceptions.fix: Planets move in elongated paths called elliptical orbits.

probe.question: If a planet's path is a circle, what is the distance from the Sun?
probe.wrong_answer: It is always the same distance.

misconceptions.root_belief: Simple shapes are more natural than complex ones.

misconceptions.statement: The Sun is a planet because it is big and round.
misconceptions.fix: The Sun is a star that produces its own heat and light, unlike planets.

probe.question: Is the Sun a planet?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is the biggest planet in the solar system.

misconceptions.root_belief: All round things in space are planets.

misconceptions.statement: The Moon produces its own light like the Sun.
misconceptions.why: The Moon looks bright in the night sky, so students assume it is a light source.
misconceptions.fix: The Moon does not have its own light; it reflects the light of the Sun.

probe.question: Why does the Moon shine at night?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is a glowing ball of fire.

misconceptions.root_belief: Visible brightness implies internal light source.

misconceptions.fix: Asteroids are rocky bodies orbiting the Sun, while meteoroids are small pieces that burn up in the atmosphere.

probe.question: What is an asteroid?
probe.wrong_answer: A star that falls from the sky.

misconceptions.root_belief: Similar sounding words have the same meaning.

misconceptions.statement: The Sun goes around the Earth, so the Earth stays still at the centre.
misconceptions.why: Everyday experience shows the Sun rising and setting while the ground feels motionless, so Earth seems fixed.
misconceptions.fix: The Earth and all other planets revolve around the Sun. The Sun only appears to move across the sky because the Earth rotates on its axis.

probe.question: Which one goes around the other: the Earth or the Sun?
probe.wrong_answer: The Sun goes around the Earth.

misconceptions.root_belief: What I see in the sky shows what really moves
misconceptions.source_hint: science education research on alternative frameworks about Earth and Sun

misconceptions.statement: All planets take one year to go around the Sun.
misconceptions.why: Students know Earth takes one year and assume the same time applies to every planet.
misconceptions.fix: Planets nearer the Sun have shorter orbits and take less time, while farther planets take much longer. Mercury takes about 88 days and Neptune about 165 years.

probe.question: How long does Jupiter take to complete one revolution around the Sun?
probe.wrong_answer: One year, the same as Earth.

misconceptions.root_belief: Earth's properties are the same for every planet

misconceptions.statement: The Sun gives light and heat only in the daytime and is off at night.
misconceptions.why: Students link the Sun's existence to when they can see it and think it switches on and off.
misconceptions.fix: The Sun always shines. Night comes when our part of the Earth faces away from the Sun because of the Earth's rotation.

probe.question: What happens to the Sun at night?
probe.wrong_answer: The Sun goes out or stops shining.

misconceptions.root_belief: Things exist only when I can see them
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on children's ideas of day and night

misconceptions.statement: The Sun is the closest star to Earth, so it is small compared to Earth.
misconceptions.why: The Sun looks like a small disc in the sky, so students judge its size by appearance.
misconceptions.fix: The Sun is a huge star, more than a million times the volume of Earth. It looks small only because it is very far away.

probe.question: Which is bigger, the Sun or the Earth?
probe.wrong_answer: The Earth is bigger because the Sun looks small.

misconceptions.root_belief: Apparent size in the sky equals real size

misconceptions.statement: Earth is the only planet that has water, so water is found nowhere else.
misconceptions.why: Earth is called the blue planet and students stretch this into thinking no other body has any water.
misconceptions.fix: Earth is the only known planet with liquid water on its surface, which is needed for life. Other bodies may have ice or vapour but not liquid water oceans.

probe.question: Is there any form of water on other planets or bodies in the solar system?
probe.wrong_answer: No, water exists only on Earth.

misconceptions.root_belief: Unique to Earth means absent everywhere else

misconceptions.statement: Earth has life because it is the closest planet to the Sun and so is the warmest.
misconceptions.why: Students assume more heat means more life, and think Earth is nearest to the Sun.
misconceptions.fix: Earth is the third planet from the Sun, not the nearest. It is at the right distance, with moderate temperature, so water stays liquid and air is present for life.

probe.question: Why is there life on Earth but not on Mercury?
probe.wrong_answer: Earth is closest to the Sun so it gets the most heat.

misconceptions.root_belief: Life needs only nearness to the Sun

misconceptions.statement: The Moon changes shape because the Earth's shadow covers part of it each night.
misconceptions.why: Students link the phases to shadows and mix them up with lunar eclipses.
misconceptions.fix: The Moon's shape does not change. We see different lit portions as the Moon revolves around Earth, so the sunlit half faces us at different angles.

probe.question: Why do we see a crescent Moon on some nights and a full Moon on others?
probe.wrong_answer: Earth's shadow falls on part of the Moon.

misconceptions.root_belief: Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's explanations of moon phases

misconceptions.statement: The asteroid belt is a thick crowded ring where asteroids keep crashing into one another.
misconceptions.why: Pictures and films show asteroid fields as packed with rocks, so students think the belt is dense.
misconceptions.fix: Asteroids lie between Mars and Jupiter in a wide belt, but they are very far apart. They orbit the Sun and rarely collide.

probe.question: What would it be like to travel through the asteroid belt?
probe.wrong_answer: It would be crowded and the rocks would keep hitting the spacecraft.

misconceptions.root_belief: Space scenes in films are accurate
